title: Neither knows: the chamber of secrets
hookLine: giving where giver and receiver don't know each other
carry: neither knows: a gift for its own sake
last: SO THEY NEVER NEED TO ASK.

cards: In the Temple in Jerusalem, Maimonides writes, there was a room called the chamber of secrets. Righteous people would go in quietly and leave something.
Poor people from good families were supported from it, just as quietly. The giver never saw who took. The one who took never saw who gave.
Maimonides points to that room when he describes the rung just below the top of his ladder.

teach.h: NOT THE GIVER, NOT THE RECEIVER.
teach.b: Neither knows. The rung, in plain English: below the highest is one who gives to the poor without knowing to whom he gives, while the poor person doesn't know from whom he takes.
Maimonides calls this doing the commandment for its own sake. First, what disappears.
The giver gets no thanks, no nod at synagogue, no quiet feeling of being owed. The receiver owes nobody: no awkward meeting in the market, no lowering of the eyes.
Second, for its own sake. Lishmah, in Hebrew. With every reward stripped away, what's left is the gift itself.
No one can give to be seen when no one can see. Third, the room today.
Something close to this rung, he says, is giving into the community's charity fund, but only if the person in charge is trustworthy, wise, and knows how to manage it properly.
Anonymous giving depends on an honest middle. Without one, the secret room is just a dark room. Fourth, why it's not the top.
The highest rung is personal: a loan, a job, a partnership, help that ends the need. Neither knows relieves need rather than ending it. One protects dignity by hiding the giver.
The other protects it by making the gift unnecessary.

teach.h: THE QUIET CHAMBER, THE OPEN DOOR.
teach.b: A community needs both kinds of room: the quiet chamber, and the open door to work.

how: Jews give through community charity funds and collection boxes, called pushkes in Yiddish, so that the giver and the receiver need not know each other.

o: a donation the giver forgets about right away
giver and receiver never learn each other's names
a gift of advice given without saying a word

p: a room in the Temple for quiet giving
only with a trustworthy person in charge

s: Maimonides makes neither-knows giving the very top rung
it's just below the top. the highest rung is a gift, loan, partnership or job that ends the need.
he connects this rung to a room in the Temple called the chamber of secrets
givers went in quietly, and the poor were supported from it quietly.
he says giving into any charity fund counts, no matter who runs it
only if the one in charge is trustworthy, wise and manages it properly.

games.q: you want to give so that neither you nor the receiver knows the other. there's a community fund. what does Maimonides say to check first?
o: that your name will be read out as a donor.
that the person in charge is trustworthy and wise.
games.why: he says giving into the fund is close to this rung, but only when the one in charge is trustworthy, wise and knows how to manage it.

practice: Think of a way to give where your name stays out of it: a trusted fund, an unsigned gift, paying for something no one will trace back to you. Then notice what part of you wants to be known for it, even a little.
Don't fight it; just see it, and let it sit beside the gift.

wordCard.voice: Neither knows. The rung just below the top of Maimonides' ladder: the giver doesn't know who receives, and the receiver doesn't know who gave, like the Temple's chamber of secrets. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the chamber of secrets, a room in the Temple where gifts were given and taken quietly.

carryVoice: Your line: neither knows: a gift for its own sake. No thanks, no debt, like the Temple's chamber of secrets. Until tomorrow.
